analysis.investment_thesis: CMS Info Systems possesses a genuine earnings record — seven consecutive years of profit growth at a 24.6% CAGR — and carries negligible debt (D/E 0.10), qualities I admire. However, at INR 318, the stock trades above my calculated Graham Number of ~INR 268 and at a P/B of 2.24, well above my 1.5 threshold, offering no meaningful margin of safety.
key_strengths: Seven unbroken years of earnings growth (net profit CAGR 24.6%), satisfying my core requirement of proven earning power
Near-debt-free balance sheet (D/E 0.10) with cash of INR 231 Cr largely offsetting the new INR 223 Cr borrowings in 2025
Consistently positive operating cash flow (5/5 years) with FY2025 FCF of INR 331 Cr — real cash, not accounting fiction
key_risks: P/B of 2.24 exceeds my 1.5 ceiling; the investor is paying INR 2.24 for every INR 1.00 of net assets — insufficient asset protection
Zero promoter ownership is deeply troubling; management has no personal capital at risk alongside shareholders
Sudden appearance of INR 223 Cr in borrowings in FY2025 (from zero prior years) warrants scrutiny — capital allocation discipline unproven under leverage
red_flags: Graham Number ~INR 268 vs. current price INR 318 — stock is trading ~19% above fair value by my formula (sqrt(22.5 × EPS ~22.6 × BVPS ~141.5))
0% promoter holding — sellers know their business better than buyers; who is left holding the bag?
No dividend data provided; a company generating INR 331 Cr FCF that does not return meaningful cash to shareholders raises questions about capital stewardship
analysis.detailed_analysis:
CMS Info Systems is a competent, cash-generative business in an essential niche — cash logistics and ATM management for Indian banks. The financial record is the strongest argument in its favor: revenue has grown from INR 978 Cr to INR 2,425 Cr over seven years (13.9% CAGR) while net profit nearly quintupled from INR 80 Cr to INR 372 Cr (24.6% CAGR). Operating cash flow has been positive in every year on record. The balance sheet is conservatively financed — until FY2025, borrowings were effectively zero. By the temperament test I apply to businesses, this one passes. The trouble, as always, is price.

My Graham Number — derived from audited earnings and book value — comes to approximately INR 268. The market is asking INR 318, a 19% premium to intrinsic value by my measure. The P/B of 2.24 also exceeds my firm ceiling of 1.5. Mr. Market is pricing in future growth, not present assets and earning power — and that is precisely where the speculative element enters. The zero promoter holding compounds my unease: when insiders own none of the equity, I must ask why. Institutional investors (FII 28.2%, DII 32.6%) are not long-term partners in the Graham sense. I would revisit this business should the price retreat toward INR 250–265, where a genuine margin of safety would exist.
